title: Attitude-Behaviour Gap Laboratory
summary: Four fictional colleagues give the same answer to "I speak up when I disagree in a team meeting", then behave differently. Predict what each of them does, then move one condition and watch behaviour change while the attitude stays put.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a measured evaluation from an action, and say what stands between them.
Explain why some intervening conditions add to the odds while opportunity gates them.
State how measurement correspondence changes an attitude-behaviour association without changing the person.
Explain why the same correlation is larger under uniform conditions than in ordinary teams.
Say what an individual-level model of behaviour represents well and what it makes harder to see.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the questionnaire is never administered to the person using the tool, and every calculation runs in the browser tab.
accessibilityNotes: Native radios, ranges and selects; no dragging and no timing. Each experiment exposes only its own controls and its own result, and the pinned primary result in experiments 2 and 3 is small (125px and 301px) so it stays in view while the controls are scrolled. The contribution chart prints each term's signed value beside its bar and is paired with a visible table, so direction never depends on fill; the scatterplot is paired with a sentence giving the correlation, the group sizes and the two group means. Every slider carries an aria-valuetext in words naming both ends of its range. Focus moves to the new experiment heading when a stage button is pressed. Changes are announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths. Experiment 2 shows one of its six condition sliders; the other five, the person selector and the correspondence control sit inside a native <details> element, and the population-level experiment sits in a second one with its own controls, so both are one keyboard step away and are announced as collapsed rather than being disabled.
readmeTopic: Four identical attitude scores, four different working lives: what stands between an evaluation and an act
simulationNotes: A small logistic model in the reasoned-action family with every coefficient printed on screen: logit = -1.30 + 2.60 x c x attitude + 1.30 x norm + 1.50 x perceived control + 1.40 x habit - 1.80 x constraint, and p = logistic(logit) x opportunity. All conditions run from 0 to 1; c is the correspondence weight of the measure (0.35 general values, 0.70 behaviour-level, 1.00 matched intention). Opportunity multiplies rather than adds, which is the structural point the tool is built on. The four colleagues are fictional; with the behaviour-level measure they come out at 82, 28, 14 and 48 per cent of occasions. Experiment 3 draws 300 simulated colleagues from a seeded mulberry32 generator (seed 20260419); the same attitude draws are reused in every cell so that no difference between cells can be a sampling difference, and only the variance of the conditions changes. The resulting correlations are 0.69, 0.84 and 0.87 under uniform conditions and 0.20, 0.35 and 0.41 in varying conditions, for the general, behaviour-level and matched measures respectively. None of these numbers is an estimate of anything and none should be quoted as an effect size; a simulation cannot test a theory.
